content: NCK1 is a cytoplasmic protein encoded by the NCK1 gene in humans. The NCK1 gene belongs to the adaptor family of proteins, specifically the non-catalytic region of tyrosine kinase adaptor protein 1. This gene was initially identified from a human melanoma cDNA library using a monoclonal antibody targeting a melanoma-associated antigen. The NCK family includes two known members in human cells (NCK1/NCKα and NCK2/NCKβ), two in mouse cells (mNCKα and mNCKβ/Grb4), and one in Drosophila (Dock, an ortholog of dreadlocks). The two murine gene products share 68% amino acid identity, with most sequence variation occurring in the linker regions between the SH3 and SH2 domains. These murine proteins are 96% identical to their human counterparts. The human NCK1 gene is located on chromosome 3 at locus 3q21, while the NCK2 gene is found on chromosome 2 at locus 2q12. The protein encoded by NCK1 is a signaling and transforming protein containing Src homology 2 (SH2) and Src homology 3 (SH3) domains. It is localized in the cytoplasm and functions as an adaptor protein, facilitating signal transduction from receptor tyrosine kinases to downstream effectors such as RAS. NCK1 has been implicated in glucose tolerance and insulin signaling, particularly in the liver of obese mice. Deletion of NCK1 reduces endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress signaling in these obese cells, which is typically elevated due to excessive fat. ER stress activates the unfolded protein response (UPR) pathway, leading to impaired glucose tolerance and insulin signaling. The inhibition of the UPR pathway, specifically through the protein IRE1α, restores glucose tolerance and insulin signaling. IRE1α is involved in the JNK pathway, which phosphorylates IRS-1, thereby blocking insulin signaling. NCK1 regulates the activation of IRE1α, and its removal disrupts this activation, linking NCK1 to the UPR and ER stress pathways in mice. Obese mice deficient in NCK1 exhibit increased insulin-induced phosphorylation of PKB (Akt) in the liver but not in adipose tissue or skeletal muscle, suggesting that the pathway is ER stress-induced in liver tissue. NCK1 has also been associated with bone mass regulation. A deficiency in NCK1, which reduces ER stress in obese mice, accelerates osteoporosis caused by mechanical unloading. This suggests that NCK1 plays a critical role in bone metabolism and that other proteins involved in bone tissue retention remain unidentified. NCK1 expression doubles during unloading-induced osteoporosis, indicating that its absence in deficient organisms leads to increased bone loss due to the inability to respond to stress, as observed in vivo. This accelerated bone loss suggests that bone metabolism is tightly regulated by multiple proteins, some of which are yet to be discovered. NCK1 is also involved in cellular remodeling through the WASp/Arp2/3 complex, coordinating actin cytoskeletal remodeling. WASp binds to the SH3 domains in the N-terminal region of NCK1. Upon activation by signals from receptor tyrosine kinases, NCK1 utilizes the WASp/Arp2/3 complex to reorganize the actin cytoskeleton, promoting cell polarization and directional migration via pseudopodia. This cytoskeletal reorganization is mediated by the relocation of various Rho GTPases to specific cellular locations, particularly the leading edge, and by strengthening bonds with extracellular matrix components to induce motion. NCK1 has been shown to interact with several proteins, including: ABL1, CBL, DNM1, DAG1, EIF2B2, EPHB1, EGFR, KHDRBS1, LCP2, MAP4K1, MAP4K4, MINK1, NCKIPSD, NEDD9, PAK1, PDGFRB, PKN2, PTK2, RASA1, RICS, RRAS, SOCS7, SOS1, TBK1, WASL, WIPF1, and WAS.
